candidateRows: Human conscience reveals violations of God's moral law, making divine judgment and Christ's substitutionary payment intelligible.
This supplies the central pro-side explanation connecting sin, deserved judgment, substitutionary atonement, and salvation.
Comfort uses the commandments and a paid-fine analogy to argue that acknowledged guilt explains how Christ can legally release sinners from punishment.
Death is the divinely imposed wage of sin and signals that every person faces judgment after death.
The claim establishes the peril from which salvation is needed and grounds the asserted seriousness of human sin.
Comfort interprets mortality as earned punishment for sin and presents death as evidence of humanity's condemned condition before divine judgment.
The gospel becomes rational once a person recognizes the seriousness of sin, repents, and trusts Christ for eternal life.
It directly answers the motion by identifying recognition of guilt as the condition under which atonement and salvation make sense.
Comfort develops the fine analogy, contrasts pride with acknowledgment of guilt, and concludes that repentance and trust bring promised eternal life.
If an omniscient God could have created otherwise, God rather than Adam and Eve bears responsibility for original sin entering the world.
The argument challenges the explanatory coherence of the gospel's foundational account of the origin and attribution of sin.
Comfort's account that human violation of God's law creates deserved guilt and judgment.
Dillahunty questions divine authority and argues that foreknowledge plus the ability to create another world shifts responsibility for the fall to God.
Inherited guilt is unjust because people are treated as culpable for conduct committed by earlier human beings.
It attacks the moral legitimacy of the inherited-sin premise that supports the claimed universal need for atonement.
Comfort's claim that all people stand guilty under God's law and deserve the death sentence.
Dillahunty compares inherited sin to receiving punishment for an act one did not commit, presenting transferred guilt as morally defective.
Jesus's sacrifice resembles blood magic and is an unnecessary loophole because a sovereign God could forgive directly.
It directly disputes both the moral sense and explanatory necessity of substitutionary sacrifice at the center of the gospel.
Comfort's paid-fine account in which Jesus's death permits God justly to release guilty sinners.
Dillahunty connects animal sacrifice to Jesus's death, argues God controls the rules, and questions why forgiveness requires self-sacrifice rather than direct pardon.
God's proposed salvation plan is needlessly inefficient if the goal is eternal fellowship with chosen people.
It challenges the gospel's explanatory sense by contrasting the alleged divine plan with a simpler means available to an omnipotent being.
Comfort's presentation of the gospel as God's coherent provision of eternal life for repentant believers.
Dillahunty argues God could create desired companions directly, while the actual narrative introduces foreseeable failure, suffering, damnation, sacrifice, and divine silence.
Moral judgments are situational rather than an exceptionless divine law written uniformly on every conscience.
The counterexample undermines Comfort's conscience-based route from ordinary moral awareness to knowledge of God's commandments.
Comfort's assertion that conscience reveals God's law and that people know lying is morally wrong.
Dillahunty denies that lying is always wrong and uses deception to protect a threatened person as an example of morally justified falsehood.
Scripture warrants the claim that people know God exists but suppress that knowledge to avoid moral responsibility.
The move defends Comfort's disputed attribution of knowledge and explains unbelief as culpable denial rather than evidential absence.
Dillahunty's denial that he knows God exists or shares Comfort's claimed conscience-based moral knowledge.
Comfort appeals to an inspired account of humanity, divine knowledge of each person, creation's declaration of God, and suppression motivated by accountability.
Atheism functions as flight from God because people prefer morally unaccountable darkness to exposure under divine law.
The argument supplies the pro side's causal explanation for rejection of the gospel and reinforces its conscience-centered account of sin.
Dillahunty's repeated denial that unbelief reflects suppressed knowledge of God or awareness of divine guilt.
Comfort interprets the prodigal son's departure as concealment from paternal judgment and analogizes atheism to avoiding exposure of morally wrongful desires.
An omniscient God who selected this universe over alternatives bears ultimate responsibility for creating the conditions in which Matt is a nonbeliever.
The argument directly challenges the moral and explanatory coherence of assigning individual blame within a world deliberately selected by an omniscient creator.
Ray's affirmation that God is omniscient and could have created a different universe.
After securing Ray's agreement about omniscience and possible alternative worlds, Matt argues that God's selection makes God ultimately responsible for the resulting nonbelief.
Divine foreknowledge or original sin does not excuse a person's serious wrongdoing, just as blaming God would fail as a defense in court.
The analogy defends personal moral accountability against Matt's claim that God's choice of world transfers ultimate responsibility away from individuals.
Matt's argument that God's selection of this universe makes God responsible for Matt's nonbelief.
Ray answers the responsibility argument by comparing it to a guilty defendant blaming God or original sin, which Ray says would not excuse the crime.
Matt's argument concerns responsibility inside Ray's theological model, where God's exhaustive choice eliminates free will, rather than denying ordinary responsibility for actions.
This clarification restores the central objection that divine selection and planning undermine the individual responsibility required by the gospel's account of judgment.
Ray's courtroom analogy portraying Matt as excusing wrongdoing by saying that God caused it.
Matt says he is not denying responsibility in reality; he is arguing internally that Ray's God chose every relevant condition and thereby displaced free will and individual responsibility.
Ray's case presupposes God as judge and supplies assertions rather than evidence, so it cannot establish that the gospel is true or even evaluate it without circular assumptions.
The move challenges the evidential and methodological foundation of the affirmative case rather than merely disputing a peripheral doctrinal detail.
Ray's appeals to other atheists and his repeated assertions about atheism, creation, and God's existence.
Matt argues that Ray begins by assuming a divine judge, refuses to examine the gospel without that assumption, and has offered neither evidence nor a developed argument.
The truth of the gospel can be known through genuine repentance, while Matt's former Christianity was a false conversion that left him resistant to the truth.
This is Ray's principal epistemic and salvific answer: experiential confirmation follows obedience to the gospel, while apostasy indicates that conversion was not genuine.
Matt's demand for a method of determining whether Ray's asserted gospel claims are actually correct.
Ray says Matt should obey the gospel and explains Matt's disbelief as the aftermath of an insincere conversion that failed under later pressures.
Although Matt now denies that anyone has an actual relationship with the risen Christ, his former Christian belief was sincere and publicly recognizable, so apostasy does not show insincerity.
The distinction directly contests the false-conversion explanation and exposes its inability to accommodate apparently sincere believers who later reject Christianity.
Ray's claim that Matt never truly repented or knew God and therefore underwent only a false conversion.
Matt concedes that he did not literally know Christ under his present view but maintains that he and those around him sincerely believed he did for years.
Designed objects are identified through comparative investigation and specific traces of agency, not by labeling every complex or structured thing a creation.
The move attacks the creation-implies-creator inference that Ray offers as proof of God, supplying an alternative evidential method for distinguishing design from nature.
Ray's claim that creation proves a creator just as a building proves a builder or a painting proves a painter.
Using dams and sculptures, Matt argues that agency is inferred by comparing designed and natural outcomes and investigating distinctive physical indications of intentional production.
Jesus's answer to the rich ruler presents keeping specified moral commandments, and ultimately relinquishing possessions and following Jesus, as the route to eternal life.
This scriptural interpretation directly challenges Ray's account of salvation by repentance and faith by appealing to Jesus's stated answer about obtaining eternal life.
Ray's earlier use of the rich-ruler encounter to support his presentation of the law and the gospel.
Matt reads the passage as having Jesus direct the ruler toward selected commandments and, for perfection, disposal of property and personal discipleship.
The rich ruler's wealth was likely fraudulent, but selling it could not earn salvation; commandments expose sin, while salvation comes by grace through repentance and faith in Jesus.
The response states the affirmative side's core account of law, grace, repentance, faith, and salvation while directly reconciling the disputed biblical passage with that account.
Matt's reading of Jesus as teaching that commandment keeping and disposal of possessions secure eternal life.
Ray highlights the instruction against fraud, infers wrongdoing behind the ruler's wealth, and argues that neither restitution nor obedience earns life because the law reveals sin and grace saves.

Evidence for a human relationship can be independently demonstrated, whereas Ray's claimed divine relationship cannot; confidence based on reasons is therefore different from faith without good reasons.
The comparison directly challenges Ray's experiential warrant for knowing God by arguing that ordinary relationships have public evidence unavailable for the asserted divine relationship.
Ray's contention that Matt merely refuses belief and that accepting a demonstrated marriage would itself require faith.
Matt rejects the claim that he simply chooses disbelief and contrasts verifiable marital relationships with God claims, defining rational confidence as grounded in demonstrable reasons.
Faith is not evidence-based confidence but an excuse for belief when no good reason can be supplied.
This distinction supplies the skeptical epistemic standard used throughout the exchange to challenge the claimed basis for Christian belief.
Ray Comfort's characterization of confidence or trust as equivalent to religious faith.
The speakers compare evidence for a marriage with evidence for a divine relationship, leading to a dispute over whether confidence and faith are equivalent.
A relationship with a spouse is demonstrable through independent evidence, whereas Ray's claimed relationship with God is not comparably demonstrable.
The comparison directly challenges Ray's analogy between ordinary interpersonal relationships and an asserted relationship with an unseen deity.
Ray Comfort's attempt to place belief in his relationship with God on the same footing as belief in his marriage.
After testing marriage certificates and spousal testimony as possible verification, Matt states that the same forms of corroboration are unavailable for God.
Scriptural inspiration attributed to God may instead originate in the believer's own mind, with no reliable external method for distinguishing competing claims.
The move challenges the explanatory reliability and public verifiability of personal revelation, a principal basis offered for Ray's divine relationship.
Ray Comfort's claim that God communicates with him daily through the words of scripture.
Ray says God speaks through scripture rather than an audible voice; Matt asks how an outsider could distinguish genuine revelation from private interpretation.
Taking God's existence, moral authority, and scripture on faith is not a sound method for reaching truth when those claims cannot be demonstrated.
This is a consolidated challenge to the explanatory foundation of the gospel account, arguing that its essential premises lack a truth-tracking basis.
Ray Comfort's instruction to repent, trust Christ, and approach scripture through faith and humility.
Following Ray's claim that scripture becomes intelligible after trusting Christ, Matt rejects assumptions about his inner state and attacks faith-based justification generally.
Natural suffering is evidence of the biblical account because disease, disaster, pain, and death are consequences of living in a fallen creation.
The move offers the evangelical account's principal explanation for apparently unjust suffering and presents that suffering as corroboration rather than disconfirmation.
The questioner's contention that childhood cancer and God's foreknowledge of Satan make God responsible and unjust.
A question invokes childhood cancer, Satan, divine foreknowledge, and responsibility; Ray broadens the issue to suffering generally and invokes the Fall.
Persistent religious disagreement results from humanity inventing gods in its own image, while the first commandment identifies a single true creator.
The argument addresses religious pluralism by preserving the exclusivity of the Christian God and explaining alternatives as human moral constructions.
The questioner's challenge that prolonged debate has produced no agreement about which god is real or whether any gods exist.
Asked why centuries of debate have not resolved God's identity or existence, Ray contrasts one creator with human-made deities lacking binding moral demands.
A creator able to make a different universe bears responsibility for foreseeable atrocities that occur in the universe it deliberately chose to create.
The argument directly contests the moral coherence of absolving an omniscient creator while assigning responsibility only to created human agents.
Ray Comfort's claim that perpetrators alone answer for atrocities and that God bears no responsibility for their actions.
Ray denies that God is responsible for Jeffrey Dahmer or Hitler and emphasizes judgment; Matt appeals to God's acknowledged ability to create differently.
God cares for fallen humanity by offering salvation through Christ's death to anyone who believes, regardless of ethnicity.
This move succinctly presents the evangelical atonement and salvation claim at the center of the debate's contested gospel account.
Matt Dillahunty's questioning of whether God cares about people whom Ray says are not God's children.
After Ray distinguishes God's children from rebellious humanity, Matt presses whether God nevertheless cares for them, prompting Ray's gospel summary.
Because God already knows who will be saved, God could have created those people with him from the outset instead of creating the present world.
The argument challenges the explanatory necessity of earthly testing, suffering, and perdition within a salvation plan governed by complete foreknowledge.
Ray Comfort's claim that God lovingly offers everlasting life through Christ to whoever believes.
Immediately after Ray describes an open offer of salvation, Matt argues that foreknowledge makes the existing route to heaven unnecessary.
Substitutionary payment may cancel a debt or repair damage, but it does not reform the wrongdoer's defective character or stop continued wrongdoing.
The analogy directly attacks substitutionary atonement by arguing that transferred payment leaves the underlying moral agent and behavioral problem unchanged.
The debt-payment analogy offered in the audience question as a model for understanding another party's payment on behalf of a wrongdoer.
An audience question asks whether third-party debt payment changes an unreliable debtor; Matt explains why compensation does not itself transform the offender.
Christianity uniquely teaches that guilty people cannot earn salvation, but may receive divine mercy through Christ's sacrificial death and resurrection.
The move directly supplies the affirmative account of sin, judgment, atonement, and salvation while distinguishing it from works-based religious systems.
The question challenges Christianity's claim to be truer than competing religions that also possess authoritative books.
During audience questions, Ray contrasts works-based religions with Christianity and argues that Christ's sacrifice permits a just God mercifully to dismiss the sinner's case.
Final punishment is just because earthly goods are divine gifts that God may withdraw from sinners at judgment, even when human reason cannot resolve every difficulty.
The response squarely defends the morality of divine judgment and hell, a central component of the disputed gospel account of sin and salvation.
The audience question challenges whether sinners can morally deserve punishment that continues without end.
Ray answers a direct moral challenge to hell by presenting ordinary pleasures as gifts from God, asserting that judgment will be right, and appealing to trust in God.
Atheism is not an explanatory worldview but a label for lacking belief in gods; reliable understanding instead comes from science, logic, evidence, and sound epistemology.
The move clarifies the skeptical side's epistemic foundation and rejects the recurring claim that atheism must itself explain reality like a comprehensive worldview.
The audience challenge alleges that Matt stands behind atheism even though atheism cannot explain what exists.
Matt distinguishes atheism from a worldview, locates his positive methods in science and reasoning, and says evidence for a god would change his atheistic status without changing those methods.
Belief in the resurrection rests on personal manifestation of the living Christ, available to anyone who repents, trusts Christ as sin-bearer, and follows him.
The move supplies Ray's principal experiential justification for the resurrection and connects that claimed verification directly to repentance, atonement, and salvation.
The audience question challenges the resurrection's basis by citing Gospel controversy and the added ending of Mark.

Ray declines to ground resurrection belief primarily in Gospel reports, instead claiming direct experiential disclosure of Christ and presenting repentance and trust as a test that carries a divine promise.
Ray's promised test of salvation is insulated from failure because any sincere seeker who remains unconvinced can be blamed for performing the test incorrectly.
This directly attacks the explanatory and evidential coherence of the offered salvation mechanism by arguing that no possible outcome is allowed to count against it.
Ray claims that repentance and trust in Christ will reveal the truth and transform the person who follows that prescription.

Matt argues that the proposed conversion test is protected from disconfirmation because continued unbelief is attributed to a hardened heart or defective effort rather than treated as contrary evidence.
Speech, identity, and personality are functions of a living brain, and their alteration through brain damage supports mortality rather than the existence of a separable soul.
The move challenges the soul and postmortem-personhood assumptions needed for Ray's account of eternal judgment, punishment, and everlasting salvation.
Ray argues that the life presently speaking through Matt is his soul and therefore a distinct enduring entity.
Matt gives a physical account of speech and personal identity, points to the effects of brain damage, and concludes that available evidence indicates the self ends with brain death.
Moral judgment should evaluate the consequences of actions for a better world rather than define wrongness through a divine creator, judge, and scriptural authority.
The move presents the skeptical side's alternative foundation for morality, directly bearing on whether the gospel's definitions of sin and judgment make moral sense.
The audience asks why theistic arguments persuade people, inviting assessment of Ray's guilt-centered religious model.

Matt says theistic appeals work partly because nearly everyone recognizes personal wrongdoing, then contrasts Ray's God-defined model with consequence-based moral evaluation aimed at improving the world.
A worldview should be accepted for correct, evidentially supported explanations, not for explaining everything; honestly leaving origins unresolved is preferable to unsupported completeness.
The move rebuts a recurring explanatory argument for theism and states a general criterion for comparing the gospel's explanations with acknowledged uncertainty.
The audience challenge asks how Matt can maintain a worldview that lacks an explanation for the universe's origin.

Matt allows several possible explanations for existence while withholding commitment, arguing that evidential quality matters more than total coverage and that claimed omniscient explanation can conceal uncertainty.
The god claim is unfalsifiable, so endless debate cannot disprove God, but belief persists because supporters accept claims that cannot be falsified and need not be evidentially supported.
The move identifies unfalsifiability as the central epistemic defect in the affirmative explanation while carefully distinguishing lack of disproof from positive support.
The audience proposes that a conclusive divine demonstration would end debate and asks whether continued debate instead implies God's nonexistence.
Matt charitably reconstructs the audience's argument, rejects continued disagreement as disproof, and explains why an unfalsifiable proposition can remain believed and debated indefinitely.
Reasonable trust must be proportioned to demonstrable evidence, whereas calling receptiveness to the gospel humility improperly treats skepticism and demands for proof as personal defects.
The response condenses the skeptical case against belief without demonstration and challenges the affirmative's tendency to explain rejection through pride rather than deficient evidence.
Ray describes people who openly receive his gospel presentation as possessing the humble heart needed to listen.
After Ray praises humble listeners, Matt reframes such receptiveness as lack of skepticism and argues that asking for a demonstration is evidential inquiry rather than pride or boastfulness.
Trust in trained professionals and regulated systems is proportioned to publicly available evidence, unlike trust in God.
The argument directly contests Ray's analogy between ordinary reliance on fallible systems and religious faith by identifying evidence and accountability as the crucial difference.
Ray's claim that pervasive reliance on pilots, doctors, machines, and other fallible things supports placing trust in God.
Ray had compared faith in God with everyday trust. Matt answers that professional and technological reliance rests on demonstrated competence, understood mechanisms, regulation, and remedies.
Claims that God reliably saves are insulated from failure by attributing every apparent counterexample to defective belief or conversion.
This identifies an alleged unfalsifiability in the pro side's salvation claim, bearing directly on whether the gospel offers a coherent and evidentially meaningful explanation.
Ray's assurance that whoever sincerely calls on God will be saved and that an apparent failure shows the person did not truly trust.

After distinguishing evidence-based reliance from faith, Matt argues that Ray adds qualifications only when tested, preserving God's reliability by classifying unsuccessful seekers as mistaken or false converts.
The skeptical case is supported by argument and evidence, whereas Ray treats unsupported religious assertions as axiomatic and dismisses criticism as mere belief.
The move crystallizes the debate's epistemic dispute by contrasting publicly defensible argument with asserted axioms and by challenging Ray to substantiate his rejection.
Ray's dismissal of Matt's evidential distinction as merely Matt's belief rather than a demonstrated criticism of religious faith.
Ray labels Matt's position a belief. Matt responds that he has supplied reasons and evidence while Ray has repeatedly asserted conclusions, then places the burden on Ray to demonstrate otherwise.
God need not be morally judged because his sinlessness and scriptural truthfulness warrant complete trust, while pervasive human wrongdoing confirms the biblical diagnosis.
The answer directly addresses whether God's goodness can be assessed and grounds the gospel's moral authority in divine sinlessness, scriptural reliability, and the claimed reality of human sin.

Asked whether anyone can judge God as just and good, Ray says trust in God's complete goodness is a prerequisite of faith and presents ordinary precautions against wrongdoing as confirmation of humanity's sinful nature.
